title: Sepsis patients whose TREWS alert was confirmed within three hours had lower mortality at five hospitals, its developers report
summary: In a five-hospital study by the TREWS developers, patients whose sepsis alert was confirmed within three hours had 3.3% absolute lower in-hospital mortality, a link that outside researchers question.
account: The Targeted Real-time Early Warning System (TREWS) is a machine-learning sepsis alert developed at Johns Hopkins University. It was deployed in the electronic health record at five hospitals in the United States, including Johns Hopkins, Howard County General Hospital and Suburban Hospital. A prospective multi-site cohort study by its developers, published in Nature Medicine on 21 July 2022, monitored 590,736 patients. The analysis focused on 6,877 patients with sepsis identified by the alert before antibiotics were started. After adjustment for presentation and severity, patients whose alert a provider confirmed within three hours had 3.3% absolute (18.7% relative) lower in-hospital mortality. They also had less organ failure and shorter stays than patients whose alert was not confirmed within three hours. No individual patient is described. Outside researchers questioned the result. In August 2022 Nemati and colleagues at the University of California San Diego wrote that the comparison is likely to be severely biased. In September 2022 Kennedy and Rudd of the University of Pittsburgh wrote that prompt confirmation may mark better care teams. Bayesian Health, which holds a license agreement with Johns Hopkins, received 510(k) clearance from the Food and Drug Administration for its sepsis flagging device on 30 April 2026. The Food and Drug Administration made no finding on mortality.
purpose: TREWS was built to identify patients developing sepsis early so that treatment can start sooner; the mortality association is its intended benefit.

ratings.reason: Cohort-level association (mortality, organ failure, length of stay) without an individually attributable event.
The study reports adjusted associations across 590,736 monitored patients, not a discrete population-level event.

ai_role.statement: TREWS flagged likely sepsis, and providers decided whether to confirm the alert and treat. The study compares patients whose alert was confirmed within 3 hours with those whose alert was not, with adjustment for presentation and severity but not for provider factors. Kennedy and Rudd (2022) note that faster confirmation may mark better care teams, and Nemati and colleagues (2022) argue that the result is likely to be severely biased. The sources include no randomized comparison of TREWS against usual care.

The authors developed TREWS at Johns Hopkins; under a license to Bayesian Health, two authors and the university receive revenue, and the university owns equity in the company.

evidence.citation: Nemati S, Shashikumar SP, Holder AL, Wardi G, Owens RL, Randomized Clinical Trials or Convenient Controls: TREWS or FALSE?, medRxiv, 9 August 2022. The authors work at the University of California San Diego and have no stated role in TREWS; two of them co-founded Healcisio, a UC San Diego startup. With data from two other health systems, they argue that the TREWS comparison does not adjust for confounding by processes of care.
evidence.title: Randomized Clinical Trials or Convenient Controls: TREWS or FALSE?
evidence.quote: Using data from over 650,000 patient encounters across two distinct healthcare systems, we show that the findings of Adams et al. are likely to be severely biased

evidence.citation: Kennedy JN, Rudd KE, A sepsis early warning system is associated with improved patient outcomes, Cell Reports Medicine 3(9):100746, 20 September 2022. The authors are critical care researchers at the University of Pittsburgh with no role in TREWS; their commentary summarizes the study and notes that the comparison may reflect better care teams.
evidence.title: A sepsis early warning system is associated with improved patient outcomes
evidence.quote: it is possible that prompt response to the alert was simply indicative of a more attentive or better resourced care team in which we would already expect improved patient outcomes

display.answer: The benefit rests on one prospective cohort study by the developers of TREWS, who compared confirmation within three hours with later or absent confirmation among 6,877 sepsis patients out of 590,736 monitored. Researchers at the University of California San Diego, in a preprint, and at the University of Pittsburgh, in a commentary, question that comparison. The Food and Drug Administration, which cleared Bayesian Health's sepsis flagging device on 30 April 2026, made no finding on mortality.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: In a five-hospital study by the TREWS developers, patients whose sepsis alert was confirmed within three hours had 3.3% absolute lower in-hospital mortality, a link that outside researchers question.
fields.account: The Targeted Real-time Early Warning System (TREWS) is a machine-learning sepsis alert developed at Johns Hopkins University. It was deployed in the electronic health record at five hospitals in the United States, including Johns Hopkins, Howard County General Hospital and Suburban Hospital. A prospective multi-site cohort study by its developers, published in Nature Medicine on 21 July 2022, monitored 590,736 patients. The analysis focused on 6,877 patients with sepsis identified by the alert before antibiotics were started. After adjustment for presentation and severity, patients whose alert a provider confirmed within three hours had 3.3% absolute (18.7% relative) lower in-hospital mortality. They also had less organ failure and shorter stays than patients whose alert was not confirmed within three hours. No individual patient is described. Outside researchers questioned the result. In August 2022 Nemati and colleagues at the University of California San Diego wrote that the comparison is likely to be severely biased. In September 2022 Kennedy and Rudd of the University of Pittsburgh wrote that prompt confirmation may mark better care teams. Bayesian Health, which holds a license agreement with Johns Hopkins, received 510(k) clearance from the Food and Drug Administration for its sepsis flagging device on 30 April 2026. The Food and Drug Administration made no finding on mortality.
